1373.title: The mind as friend
1373.hook: the mind can be enemy or friend; the Word makes it a friend
1373.howItsDone: Hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib speak directly to the mind, 'O my mind', and Sikhs use the Guru's Word and repetition of the Name, such as Waheguru, to steady it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ego is not you. Haumai is fog on the mirror, not the face. Your line: not self-hatred.

Three in the morning, and somebody in your head is talking. The bill you forgot. The thing you said at dinner. The email you haven't answered. A list of what might go wrong tomorrow, read out loud, twice. It's like a roommate who never sleeps and never runs out of news. You can argue with it, or try to drown it out. The Gurus try a third way. In the Granth, hymns turn to that restless roommate and speak to it directly, almost tenderly. O my mind.
screen: `3 A.M. AND SOMEONE IS TALKING.` → `ARGUE, OR DROWN IT OUT?` → `A THIRD WAY: O MY MIND.`

segments.voice: Man, said like mun, is the mind in the Granth: not only the thinking part, but the restless inner self that wants, fears, wanders and chooses. In year one you met it running off in the middle of a prayer. The Granth is honest that the man can chase everything shiny and drag a person with it. In the Japji, Guru Nanak puts it in four words, man jeetai jag jeet: win the mind, and you win the world. Some readers hear jeet as conquer; some as win over, the way you'd win over a skeptical friend. Either way, the struggle is real, and it's inside. Then the mind spoken to as a friend. In Raag Asa, Guru Amar Das addresses it with something close to respect. In paraphrase: O my mind, you are the form of the light; recognize your own source. He doesn't call it garbage. He reminds it who it is. What turns an enemy into a friend? In the Granth, the answer keeps coming back to the shabad, the Guru's Word. A mind with nothing to hold grabs at everything. A mind given the Word has somewhere to rest. A bored dog chews the furniture, and lies down calm once it has a job. The Gurus don't throw the mind out of the house. They give it work. So the line between enemy and friend isn't about having a noisy mind. It's about what the mind is given to hold. Befriend the mind.
screen: `MAN: THE RESTLESS INNER SELF.` · `WIN THE MIND, WIN THE WORLD.` · `O MIND, YOU ARE THE FORM OF LIGHT.` · `GIVE THE MIND THE WORD TO HOLD.` · then, large: `BEFRIEND THE MIND.`

segments.voice: Let the mind do whatever it's doing, and greet each thought the way you'd greet a friend at the door: oh, it's you. Then hand it one thing to hold, Waheguru said softly on the breath if you pray, or the breath itself if you don't. When it wanders, and it will, don't scold it; just say, O my mind, come back.
Man. The mind: the restless inner self that can pull a person away or walk beside them, and that the Guru addresses as the form of light. Today's word.
Your line: befriend the mind. The restless roommate can become a friend. See you tomorrow.

1374.title: Surat: attention
1374.hook: surat is attention; where attention goes, life follows
1374.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of joining surat, attention, to the Guru's Word, and practices like listening to kirtan and repeating the Name are ways of returning wandering attention to the One.

segments.voice: Yesterday, man, the mind, and the Guru speaking to it: O my mind. Your line: befriend the mind.

A pot of milk on the stove. You're watching it, and it sits there doing nothing, the way milk does. Your phone buzzes. You glance down, answer one message, maybe two. When you look up, the milk has climbed the pot and is pouring over onto the flame. Nothing about the milk changed. Nothing about the stove changed. The only thing that moved was where you were looking. Yesterday was the mind. Today is the part of the mind that decides where to look.
screen: `MILK ON THE STOVE.` → `ONE GLANCE AT THE PHONE.` → `ONLY YOUR LOOKING MOVED.`

segments.voice: Surat, said like soo-rut, is attention or awareness in the Granth: the inner faculty that goes out toward something and stays with it. If the man is the whole restless inner self, surat is its gaze. Early in the Japji, Guru Nanak gives a run of stanzas that each begin with one word, suniai, by listening. By listening, he says, sorrow and wrongdoing fall away; by listening, a person comes to know the earth and the heavens. That isn't casual hearing with one ear on the phone. It's attention, whole and turned toward the Word. And attention can be trained. In the realm of effort, which we met three days back, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase: there, surat is shaped, along with understanding, mind and intellect. Shaped, the way a potter shapes clay or a smith shapes metal. So attention isn't a fixed amount you were born with. It can be worked on, slowly, like a muscle or a craft. Where attention goes, life follows. A day isn't really made of hours. It's made of what you looked at during them. The milk on the stove is a small picture of a large truth: a marriage, a friendship, a child, a prayer, all boil over or go cold depending on where the surat sits. Sikh practice keeps returning the surat to the Name, again and again, gently. Attention is life.
screen: `SURAT: THE MIND'S GAZE.` · `SUNIAI: BY LISTENING.` · `IN THE REALM OF EFFORT, SURAT IS SHAPED.` · `WHERE ATTENTION GOES, LIFE FOLLOWS.` · then, large: `ATTENTION IS LIFE.`

segments.voice: Put your whole surat on the air coming in at the nose, cool, and going out, warm; that's the whole job. When attention slides off to a list or a worry, notice where it went, without a lecture, and bring it back the way you'd turn back to the stove. If you pray, let Waheguru ride on the breath.
Surat. Attention, awareness: the mind's gaze, which the Japji says is shaped in the realm of effort. Today's word.
Your line: attention is life. The milk only boils over when you look away. Same time tomorrow.

1375.title: The Word as Guru
1375.hook: the Guru is not a body but the Word
1375.howItsDone: Sikhs bow before the Guru Granth Sahib as the living Guru, understanding the Guru to be the Word, the bani, rather than a human body, and take daily guidance by reading from it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, surat: attention, the mind's gaze, shaped like clay. Your line: attention is life.

A gathering of yogis, men who had left the world behind to master the body and the breath. A traveler walks into their circle, and they start testing him. Who are you? Where do you come from? What path are you on? You met these yogis on their mountain back in year one. Their conversation is in the Granth, a long hymn called Siddh Gosht, the talk with the Siddhas. Near its heart, they ask him straight out: who is your guru? Whose disciple are you? The traveler is Guru Nanak.
screen: `A CIRCLE OF YOGIS.` → `WHO ARE YOU? WHAT PATH?` → `WHO IS YOUR GURU?`

segments.voice: For a seeker in the yogis' circle, a guru would be a person: a teacher you sat before, served and followed. Guru Nanak's answer, in paraphrase: the shabad, the Word, is the guru, and the surat, attention tuned to its sound, is the disciple. Yesterday's word is right there in the answer. The disciple isn't a body at a teacher's feet. It's attention, turned toward the Word. And the guru isn't a body either. Guru Ram Das says it plainly. In paraphrase: the bani is the Guru, and the Guru is the bani, and within the bani are all the nectars. Bani is the Word as it comes through the Gurus' hymns. He doesn't say the bani is like the Guru, or speaks for the Guru. He says it is the Guru. Think what that means. A teacher in a body can be far away, asleep, busy, or gone. A teacher who is the Word can be opened at dawn, sung in a kitchen, remembered in a hospital waiting room. It doesn't age. And it doesn't flatter: bring it a question, and it answers in its own words, not the ones you hoped for. So when Sikhs bow before the Guru Granth Sahib, they understand themselves to be bowing to the Word, not to paper and ink. The word teaches.
screen: `THE YOGIS ASK: WHO IS YOUR GURU?` · `THE WORD IS GURU; ATTENTION, DISCIPLE.` · `THE BANI IS THE GURU.` · `A TEACHER ALWAYS IN THE ROOM.` · then, large: `THE WORD TEACHES.`

segments.voice: Hold one line from the Granth you already know, and if none comes, take the opening, Ik Onkar, One Creator. Sit with it the way you'd sit before a teacher, ask it one honest question about your day, and keep your surat on the line without making up an answer. Some days a line says something; some days it just keeps you company.
The Word as Guru. In the Siddh Gosht, the shabad is the guru and attention is the disciple; Guru Ram Das says the bani is the Guru. Today's word.
Your line: the word teaches. A teacher who is always in the room. Until tomorrow.

1376.title: Granth and Panth
1376.hook: scripture and community together carry the Guru
1376.howItsDone: Sikhs gather as sangat in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib, and speak of the Guru as present in both the scripture and the Khalsa Panth, in the phrase Guru Granth, Guru Panth.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Word as Guru: the shabad is the guru, and attention is the disciple. Your line: the word teaches.

Stand at the back of a gurdwara hall and look forward. At the front, on a raised platform under a canopy, the Guru Granth Sahib, wrapped in cloth, someone sitting behind it waving a whisk. Now look down. Between you and the Granth, rows of people sitting on the floor: grandmothers, teenagers, a man still in his work uniform, a toddler wandering between laps. A book and a crowd. Yesterday, the Guru was the Word. Today, the Word doesn't travel alone.
screen: `AT THE FRONT: THE GRANTH.` → `ON THE FLOOR: THE PEOPLE.` → `A BOOK AND A CROWD.`

segments.voice: Granth means the book, the scripture: yesterday's Word, given a body of pages. Panth means the path, and by extension the people who walk it together, the Sikh community. Sikh tradition remembers that Guru Gobind Singh named no human successor. Instead, tradition says, he passed the guruship to the Granth and to the Panth, the Khalsa community. Sikhs sum it up in a short phrase: Guru Granth, Guru Panth. The Guru as book. The Guru as people. What makes a crowd a congregation? Guru Nanak asks it in Sri Raag. In paraphrase: how is the true congregation known? And he answers: it is where the One Name is spoken. So the sangat isn't holy because of who's in it, or how important they are. It's holy because of what's spoken there. Why do the two need each other? A book on a shelf with nobody reading it is silent. A crowd with nothing at the center can drift anywhere, toward whoever is loudest. Together, each keeps the other honest. The people read and sing the Granth, so the Word has a voice. The Granth holds the people to something older and steadier than any one of them. Tradition says that when Sikhs gather to decide serious matters, they do it in the Guru's presence, with the Granth in the room. Book and people.
screen: `GRANTH: THE BOOK. PANTH: THE PEOPLE.` · `GURU GRANTH, GURU PANTH.` · `WHERE THE NAME IS SPOKEN.` · `EACH KEEPS THE OTHER HONEST.` · then, large: `BOOK AND PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the people who have sat beside you in something good, a family table, a service, a hospital room, a circle of friends, and see them one by one until the room fills up. Then breathe as if you were all breathing together, and if you pray, let Waheguru be the word spoken in that room.
Granth and Panth. The scripture and the community, which together, Sikh tradition says, carry the Guru. Today's word.
Your line: book and people. The Word has a voice when people sing it. See you tomorrow.

1377.title: Miri and piri as thought
1377.hook: spiritual and worldly life held together, not split
1377.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of miri and piri, worldly and spiritual authority, as held together, remembered in Guru Hargobind's two swords and in the Akal Takht facing the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Granth and Panth: the Guru carried by a book and by a people. Your line: book and people.

Two swords, worn at once. That's how Sikh tradition remembers Guru Hargobind on the day he took up the guruship: one sword at each side. You met him and his two swords in year one. When people asked why, the answer came in a pair of words: one sword for miri, one for piri. It's easy to live as if life comes in two drawers: one for the job, the rent, the news, who does the dishes; another, smaller, for prayer or quiet. Today is about refusing the two drawers. Not the swords themselves, but the thought behind them.
screen: `TWO SWORDS, WORN AT ONCE.` → `MIRI. PIRI.` → `NOT TWO DRAWERS.`

segments.voice: Miri is worldly authority: the life of rule, justice, work, the public square. Piri is spiritual authority: the life of prayer, the Word, the inner path. Alongside the two swords, tradition says Guru Hargobind raised the Akal Takht, a seat of worldly authority, facing the Harmandir, the house of prayer. Two buildings, looking at each other. Not one behind the other, not one in another city. Facing. The idea didn't start with the swords. Guru Arjan, in the var in Raag Gujri, says it with ordinary words. In paraphrase: meeting the true Guru, a person finds the complete way, and is set free while laughing, playing, dressing and eating. Notice the verbs. Laughing. Playing. Getting dressed. Eating. Liberation isn't kept in a separate room for special occasions. It happens in the middle of the ordinary. So what does the thought ask? If miri and piri belong together, prayer has to show up at work, and work has to be done as if the Guru were watching. Sikh teachers read the two swords as a call to care about justice as a spiritual duty, and to keep the inner life awake while doing it. A prayer that never touches how you treat people stays in the drawer. A public life with no inner life loses its way. The thought refuses both. Both together.
screen: `MIRI: THE WORLD. PIRI: THE SPIRIT.` · `TWO BUILDINGS, FACING.` · `FREE WHILE LAUGHING AND EATING.` · `PRAYER AT WORK; WORK AS PRAYER.` · then, large: `BOTH TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Picture the next ordinary task you'll do, dishes, an email, a drive, a diaper, a spreadsheet, and see yourself doing it. Without changing the task at all, carry this same breath and quiet into it, with Waheguru in the back of your mind if you pray. Same task, no drawer at all.
Miri and piri as thought. Worldly life and spiritual life held together, not split: two swords, two buildings facing, one life. Today's word.

1378.title: Seva as spirituality
1378.hook: service is not a side activity; it is the path
1378.howItsDone: Sikhs do seva in gurdwaras by cooking and serving langar, washing dishes, cleaning and minding shoes, and outside them through volunteer service, understood as a spiritual practice rather than a side activity.

segments.voice: Yesterday, miri and piri: two swords, two buildings facing, one life. Your line: both together.

At a gurdwara door, you take off your shoes. Someone behind a counter takes them, slides them onto a rack, and hands you a token. When you come out, they find your pair and hand it back, sometimes wiped clean. You met that counter on day eight. Who's behind it? Nobody you hired. A college student, a retired engineer, a shopkeeper on his day off, a grandmother who has done it for years. Not paid, not there to be noticed, handling strangers' shoes, and content to be there. Today asks why that counter sits close to the center of Sikh spiritual life.
screen: `SHOES AT THE DOOR.` → `WHO IS BEHIND THE COUNTER?` → `NOT PAID. CONTENT TO BE THERE.`

segments.voice: Seva is selfless service: work done for others with no wage and no score kept. In a gurdwara it looks like cooking and serving in the langar, washing dishes, sweeping floors, minding shoes. Outside, it's anything done for someone who needs it. In Sri Raag, Guru Nanak puts it plainly. In paraphrase: earn service here in the world, and you'll be given a seat in the Lord's court. Notice where the service happens: in the world. Not after. Not somewhere holier. Here, at the shoe counter, at the stove. Tradition tells a story. During a battle, a Sikh named Bhai Ghanaiya went across the field with a water skin, giving water to the wounded, including soldiers from the other side. Some Sikhs complained to Guru Gobind Singh. When the Guru asked him why, tradition says, Ghanaiya answered that he saw no enemy, only the Guru's face in everyone. And the Guru gave him ointment as well, so he could dress their wounds too. Why is seva the path and not a side activity? It works on the very thing we met a few days ago: haumai, ego. It's hard to hold onto I, me, mine while you're scrubbing someone else's pot. So seva isn't a break from prayer. Sikhs speak of it as a form of prayer: the hands remembering what the lips say. The hope is service without the self in the way: no photo, no thank-you required. Service is the path.
screen: `SEVA: SERVICE, NO WAGE, NO SCORE.` · `EARN SERVICE HERE, IN THE WORLD.` · `BHAI GHANAIYA'S WATER SKIN.` · `HANDS THAT LOOSEN HAUMAI.` · then, large: `SERVICE IS THE PATH.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small act of service nobody would ever thank you for, a dish in the sink, a neighbor's bin, a message to someone who is struggling, and picture doing it slowly, with care, the way someone at the counter hands back a stranger's shoes. Notice any part of you that wants credit, and let it rest. If you pray, offer the act quietly with Waheguru.
Seva as spirituality. Selfless service, done in the world, not beside the path but as the path itself. Today's word.
Your line: service is the path. The hands remember what the lips say. Rest well.

1379.title: The householder's path
1379.hook: the Gurus chose family life over renunciation
1379.howItsDone: Sikh teaching honors the householder's path, marrying, working and raising a family in the world, in the pattern tradition remembers from Guru Nanak's life at Kartarpur.

segments.voice: Yesterday, seva: the shoe counter and Bhai Ghanaiya's water skin. Your line: service is the path.

Back to the circle of yogis, the Siddhas of the Siddh Gosht. These were men who had walked away from everything: wives, children, fields, money, houses. To them, a person tied to a family was tied down. And here is Guru Nanak in front of them, a man tradition remembers with a wife and sons, who would go home and farm. In the janamsakhis, the old stories of his life, the yogis invite him to join them, to take up their dress and their road. The door to the renouncer's life is wide open. Which way does he turn?
screen: `THE YOGIS LEFT EVERYTHING.` → `A GURU WITH A FAMILY.` → `THE DOOR IS OPEN.`

segments.voice: Grihasth means the householder's life: marriage, children, work, a kitchen, bills, neighbors. To the yogis, the high road to God meant leaving all that behind. In the Siddh Gosht itself, Guru Nanak answers with a picture. In paraphrase: as the lotus stays untouched in the water, and the duck swims on the stream without its feathers getting soaked, so a person can live in the world with attention on the Word. The lotus doesn't leave the pond. It just isn't drowned by it. In Raag Suhi he says it another way, in paraphrase: in the midst of the soot, stay spotless. The soot is everyday life, the smoke of the kitchen and the market. The teaching isn't to run from the smoke. It's to stay clean inside it. And the life he chose? Tradition says Guru Nanak, after his travels, settled at Kartarpur, the farm you met in year one, worked the fields, and lived among family and sangat. Tradition remembers the Gurus after him living in the world too, not in caves. So Sikh teaching sets no monk's life above the householder's: holiness is meant to happen at a kitchen table, in a marriage, while raising children. That isn't the easy road. A cave has no toddlers. This week walked the same road: the mind made a friend, attention, the Word as Guru, book and people, two swords, the shoe counter, and now the home. Holiness at home.
screen: `GRIHASTH: THE HOUSEHOLDER'S LIFE.` · `THE LOTUS STAYS IN THE POND.` · `SPOTLESS IN THE SOOT.` · `KARTARPUR: FIELDS AND FAMILY.` · then, large: `HOLINESS AT HOME.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the people you share a home with, or the people you'd call home if you live alone, and see each face. For each, ask what small thing would make their day lighter, a meal, a call, a chore taken off their list, and hold them as you breathe, the way a lotus holds still on moving water. If you pray, hold them with Waheguru.
Grihasth. The householder's life of family, work and home, which the Gurus lived as a path to the One. Today's word.
Your line: holiness at home. The lotus stays right there in the pond. That's the week.
